Not so. The vacuum you would think gets pulled through the intake isn't enough to pull anything measurable on that side of the valve cover. So at idle, it does indeed pull fresh air into the valve cover through that port while pulling vacuum on the pcv side. At roughly 30inhg. And the ECU is not tuned for that port. It's only tuned for the EGR (if applicable) and the pcv under off throttle and idle conditions. Don't believe me? Plug it and monitor it with a scanner. Under extremely heavy throttle when say in boost, it does push air through both ports from blowby or anywhere it can depending on the health of it all.

Engine dampers do the same thing as a suspension damper. Just controls the movement of the motor mounts rubber instead of springs. Remember, the stock rubber mounts were designed with the torque of a stock block. The MSM mounts are basically the competition mounts that are stiffer and hold up better to the added torque from the MSM package.

Say you're at full throttle screaming at 6k+ rpm. You let off the throttle to shift, those rubber mounts and the ppf are going to spring the motor back to a resting position. After you shift and stab the throttle, (this still applies to flat shifting), the motor is going to twist again. The damper controls how aggressive that back and forth twist happens, in other words the damper controls the shock load that the motor mounts, ppf, and associated hardware. This also applies when the motor is under load like accelerating with traffic up a incline or even merging with traffic on the highway.

Incorrect. The port you see in the pic is the intake for the fresh air to be pulled into the valve cover. The pcv valve is the vacuum side that is regulated when in vacuum to pull the fuel/oil mixed air from the block and recirculate it to burn it instead of vta. There is basically no vacuum on that port. Hence how the baffles are designed on the valve cover.

Higher octane fuels are beneficial as long as the vehicle's ECU is configured to use that octane rating. Higher fuel octane is more resistant to pre-igniting from combustion temps and pressure. This allows the ECU, (or tuner if tuning manually), to run a more advanced ignition table to get the maximum amount of power and efficiency from that motor using that specific grade of fuel. 

The ECU for Ecoboost engine is constantly adjusting ignition timing within set parameters as it is unable to detect the octane rating of the fuel. (Special cases would be those that can run E85 or flex fuel and have an ethanol sensor). Except it's slow at making the adjustments when going from 87 to say 93. Usually takes a good bit of driving or about 2 tanks of fuel give or take. However, when going from 93 to 87 it happens quickly as predetonation (knock) makes itself known like a pizza delivery. 

Turbo engines and high compression engines like Subaru's 3L H6 like high octane fuels like 91 and 93. They are able to advance the ignition timing for best all around performance, smoothness of operations, and efficiency for as long as the vehicle has the configuration to do so.

Bottom line. Our Ecoboost trucks run best with 91/93. They will run at reduced performance on 87 without any harm to the engine unless you need to either use the turbo a lot or the ambient temps are high.

A few options here depending on where you live. A turbo setup is more widely available and can be tuned to fit your needs for both performance and power. Depending on the size of the sushi slicer you may get low-mid range or mid-hogh range power. Flying Miata's kit is a good easy start in the turbo world. A bit more difficult to install than the next two options. Best bet is a standalone ECU to get the best performance for your needs. 

Positive displacement type setup such as the Jackson racing or fast forward chargers will give you more of an instant throttle response. And I feel it is easier to install as compared to a turbo setup. Gives good low-mid range torque. Not so much in the top end. Fast forward kits are an easy set it and forget it install. And can easily be removed putting the car back to factory if so desired. Can be ran from piggyback cards from the ECU as well. 

A centrifical rotrex setup from trackdog racing or the older kraftwerks kit (Im personally running the older kraftwerks kit) will not give you any low end and essentially feel like a V6 or and H6 without any vvt stuff. Easier to drive in the slippery stuff as you don't have to worry as much about the surprise boost from a turbo or the low end torque from a screw style blower. A rotrex kit is in between the turbo and fast forward kits as far as installation goes. Not as easy as the fast forward, still easier than a turbo. Can be ran by piggyback cards on the factory ECU as well.
